questions.question: Which of the following correctly arranges the brainstem nuclei from medial to lateral in the brainstem?

options.A: Oculomotor nucleus → Trochlear nucleus → Edinger Westphal nucleus
options.B: Hypoglossal nucleus → Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus → Nucleus tractus solitarius
options.C: Motor nuclei of Trigeminal → Motor nuclei of Facial → Abducent nucleus
options.D: Nucleus ambiguus → Hypoglossal nucleus → Nucleus tractus solitarius

explanation.text: The structures passing from medial to lateral in the central grey matter is Hypoglossal nucleus → Dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus → Nucleus tractus solitarius Oculomotor nucleus → Trochlear nucleus → Edinger Westphal nucleus (Option A): Edinger Westphal lies dorsal to the oculomotor nucleus and not lateral.
**Motor nuclei of Trigeminal → Motor nuclei of Facial → Abducent nucleus (Option C):** The motor nucleus of the facial nerve lies ventrolateral to the abducent nucleus.
**Nucleus ambiguus → Hypoglossal nucleus → Nucleus tractus solitarius (Option D):** Hypoglossal nuclei are medial to Nucleus Ambiguus.

questions.question: Which nuclei belong to the Special Somatic Afferent (SSA) column?

options.B: Sensory nucleus of the trigeminal nerve
options.C: Hypoglossal and abducens nuclei

explanation.text: Cochlear and vestibular nuclei are part of the SSA column, carrying special senses of hearing and balance.

**Neural column Nuclei and Cranial Nerves GSE (General Somatic Efferent) (Option C ruled out):** SVE (Special Visceral Efferent) (Option D ruled out) GVE (General Visceral Efferent) GVA/SVA (General/Special Visceral Efferent) GSA (General Somatic Afferent) (Option B ruled out) SSA (Special Somatic Afferent) (Option A) Oculomotor nucleus (III) Trochlear nucleus (IV) Abducent nucleus (VI) Hypoglossal nucleus (XII) Motor nucleus of Trigeminal Nerve (V) Motor nucleus of the facial nerve (VII) Nucleus ambiguus (IX, X, XI) Edinger Westphal nucleus (III) Superior salivatory nucleus (VII) Inferior salivatory nucleus (IX) Dorsal nucleus of Vagus (X) Nucleus Tractus Solitarius (GVA - IX, X) (SVA - VII, IX) Sensory nuclei of Trigeminal Nerve (V, IX, X) Vestibular nuclei (VIII) Cochlear nuclei (VIII) The lateral geniculate nucleus of the thalamus (II). Olfactory bulb (I) Mnemonic: Rule of 12: Any nucleus that is inclusive of 12 is medial. It includes nuclei III, IV, VI and XII. The rest are lateral. Rule of M: 3 primary medial tracts of the Brainstem. Includes Motor Tract (Corticospinal Tract), Medial Lemniscus and Medial Longitudinal Fasciculus. Rule of S: Lateral or “side” tracts. Includes Spinothalamic tract, Sympathetic tract and spinocerebellar tracts. B- Branchial Motor, CST-Corticospinal, STT- Spinothalamic, ML- Medial Lemniscus, Sm- Somatic motor, Sp-Special sensory, Ss- Somatic sensory Section through medulla showing arrangement of cranial nerve nuclei

questions.question: Which artery is most commonly occluded, leading to medial medullary syndrome and lateral pontine syndrome, respectively?

options.C: Anterior spinal artery, AICA

explanation.text: Anterior Spinal Artery: Its occlusion leads to medial medullary syndrome, resulting in contralateral hemiplegia, loss of vibration and position sense, and tongue paralysis on the same side. AICA (Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery): Occlusion leads to lateral pontine syndrome, causing symptoms like facial paralysis, vertigo, nystagmus, and ataxia.

Medial Medullary Syndrome (Dejerine Syndrome) Cause: Occlusion of the anterior spinal artery Features: Contralateral Hemiplegia: Due to damage to the medullary pyramid. Loss of Vibration and Position Sense: Resulting from damage to the medial lemniscus. Tongue Paralysis (Same Side): Caused by injury to the hypoglossal (XII) cranial nerve.

Lateral Inferior Pontine Syndrome Cause: Occlusion of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery (AICA) On Side of Lesion: Nystagmus, Vertigo, Nausea, Vomiting, Oscillopsia: Due to vestibular nerve/nucleus involvement. Facial Paralysis Impaired Conjugate Gaze: Involvement of the center for lateral gaze. Deafness and Tinnitus: Related to the auditory nerve or cochlear nucleus.

Ataxia: Affecting the middle cerebellar peduncle and cerebellar hemisphere. Impaired Sensation Over Face: Due to involvement of the descending tract and nucleus of the fifth nerve. On Side Opposite Lesion: Impaired Pain and Thermal Sensation: Involving the spinothalamic tract over one-half of the body, which may include the face.

**Anterior cerebral artery, PICA (Option A):** Anterior Cerebral Artery: Occlusion affects the medial frontal and parietal lobes, causing contralateral leg weakness and sensory loss, but does not cause the medial medullary syndrome. PICA: Occlusion leads to lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome), not lateral pontine syndrome.

**Posterior cerebral artery, Basilar artery (Option B):** Posterior Cerebral Artery: Occlusion affects the occipital lobe, causing visual field deficits and sensory disturbances, but not medial medullary syndrome. Basilar Artery: Occlusion leads to various brainstem syndromes, but is not specifically linked to lateral pontine syndrome.

**Vertebral artery, Superior cerebellar artery (Option D):** Vertebral Artery: Occlusion affects posterior circulation, causing various syndromes, but not medial medullary syndrome. Superior Cerebellar Artery: Occlusion primarily impacts the cerebellum and
brainstem, but does not cause lateral pontine syndrome.

questions.question: Which arteries supply the posterior region of the superior medulla and pons respectively?

options.A: Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery and Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery
options.C: Anterior Spinal Artery and Posterior Spinal Artery
options.D: Superior Cerebellar Artery and Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery

explanation.text: Blood supply of Medulla Oblongata: Caudally Anterior-Medial Supply: Anterior Spinal Artery (Option C ruled out) Posterior-Lateral Supply: Posterior Spinal Artery Superiorly Lateral Supply: Vertebral Artery (Option B ruled out) Anterior Supply: Basilar Artery branches Posterior Supply: Posterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (PICA) Blood supply of Pons: Main Supply: Pontine branches of the Basilar Artery Posterior-Lateral Supply: Branches of the Superior Cerebellar Artery (Option D ruled out) and the Anterior Inferior Cerebellar Artery (AICA)

questions.question: Which artery supplies the posterior region of the midbrain?

options.C: Posterior Cerebral Artery

explanation.text: Superior Cerebellar Artery provides significant blood supply to the posterior region of the midbrain Midbrain Blood Supply: Anterior-Medial Supply: branches of the Basilar artery (Option A ruled out) Anterior-Lateral Supply: branches of the Posterior Choroidal arteries and Quadrigeminal artery from the Posterior Cerebral Artery (Option B & C ruled out) Posterior Supply: Quadrigeminal Artery and Superior Cerebellar Artery

questions.question: The baroreceptor reflex that helps regulate blood pressure involves general visceral afferent (GVA) fibres from which of the following receptors and pathways?

options.A: Carotid body via the glossopharyngeal nerve
options.B: Aortic bodies via the vagus nerve
options.C: Carotid sinus via the vagus nerve
options.D: Pulmonary arteries via the glossopharyngeal nerve

explanation.text: The aortic bodies detect changes in blood pressure and relay sensory input through GVA fibres of the vagus nerve, contributing to the baroreceptor reflex. Baroreceptor Reflex: Baroreceptors in the aortic arch and carotid sinus monitor blood pressure changes. GVA fibres from the aortic arch transmit signals via the vagus nerve (X), and from the carotid sinus via the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX).

The brainstem's nucleus tractus solitarius (NTS) receives signals from GVA fibres. GVE fibres originating from the vagus nerve (X) from the dorsal motor nucleus mediate parasympathetic responses. They adjust heart rate by influencing the sinoatrial (SA) node, AV node, myocardium and other cardiac structures, helping to lower blood pressure when necessary.
**Carotid body via the glossopharyngeal nerve (Option A):** Carotid body detects gases, not pressure; the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) relates to baroreceptors in the carotid sinus.
**Carotid sinus via the vagus nerve (Option C):** While the carotid sinus does detect blood pressure changes, it transmits signals via the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX), not the vagus nerve.

**Pulmonary arteries via the glossopharyngeal nerve (Option D):** Pulmonary arteries have baroreceptors, but they are transmitted via the vagus nerve (CN X), not the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX), which mainly serves the carotid body and sinus.

questions.question: The nucleus of the solitary tract receives ______ sensations from the carotid body and carotid sinus primarily through _____ nerve.

options.C: General Visceral Afferent; Glossopharyngeal nerve

explanation.text: The nucleus of the solitary tract receives general visceral afferent sensations from the carotid body and carotid sinus primarily through the glossopharyngeal nerve (IX). The glossopharyngeal nerve (cranial nerve IX) carries sensory information from the carotid body (chemoreceptor) and carotid sinus (baroreceptor) to the nucleus of the solitary tract, which is involved in regulating blood pressure and respiratory responses.

Nucleus of Tractus Solitarius It is a composite nucleus located in the medulla. Its functions are: General Visceral Afferent (Lower Part): Receives visceral sensations. Glossopharyngeal nerve (IX): From tonsil, pharynx, posterior tongue, carotid body, and carotid sinus.

Vagus nerve (X): From the pharynx, larynx, trachea, oesophagus, and thoracic/abdominal viscera. (Option A ruled out) Special Visceral Afferent (Upper Part): Receives taste sensations. Facial nerve (VII): Anterior two-thirds of tongue and palate (except circumvallate papillae). (Option B ruled out) The glossopharyngeal nerve (IX): Posterior one-third of the tongue, including circumvallate papillae. Vagus nerve (X): Posterior tongue and epiglottis.

**Special somatic efferent; Trigeminal nerve (Option D):** Special somatic efferent fibers are related to the motor innervation of certain muscles, while the trigeminal nerve (CN V) primarily carries sensory information (touch, pain) from the face and does not innervate the carotid body or sinus.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the jaw jerk reflex is false?

options.A: It is a spinal reflex initiated by tapping the jaw.
options.B: It involves the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus as an integration centre.
options.C: The efferent pathway includes the mandibular nerve.
options.D: It is a monosynaptic reflex involving a single synapse.

explanation.text: The jaw jerk reflex is a deep tendon reflex with supraspinal involvement which is initiated by tapping the jaw. Masseter reflex or Jaw jerk reflex It is a deep tendon reflex. The reflex is initiated by tapping the midline of the mandible, which rapidly stretches the jaw-closing muscles (masseter, temporalis, medial pterygoid). The stretch activates muscle spindle afferents, which are sensory receptors in the muscles.

Afferent pathway: Muscle spindle afferents → Mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve. Integration centre (Relay): Mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus. (Option B ruled out) Efferent pathway: Motor nucleus of the trigeminal nerve → Mandibular nerve. (Option C ruled out) This results in the contraction of these jaw-closing muscles and finally closure of the jaw.

The jaw jerk reflex is the only significant supraspinal monosynaptic reflex due to its relay in the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus. (Option D ruled out) The jaw jerk reflex can be tested in neurological examinations to assess the integrity of the trigeminal nerve and the brainstem pathways.

questions.question: Which of the following nuclei of the trigeminal nerve is primarily responsible for proprioceptive sensations from the muscles of mastication?

options.C: Mesencephalic Nucleus

explanation.text: Mesencephalic Nucleus is located around the cerebral aqueduct and carries proprioceptive impulses from the muscles of mastication, facial, and extraocular muscles. The trigeminal nerve has four nuclei as follows: Main Sensory Nucleus Located in the posterior part of the pons, lateral to the motor nucleus. Continuous below with the spinal nucleus. Spinal Nucleus Extends from the pons to the second cervical segment of the spinal cord.

Receives sensations of pain and temperature. (Option B ruled out) Mesencephalic Nucleus Located in the lateral part of the grey matter around the cerebral aqueduct. Receives proprioceptive impulses from muscles of mastication, facial, and extraocular muscles. Motor Nucleus Located in the pons, medial to the main sensory nucleus.

Controls muscles of mastication, tensor tympani, tensor veli palatini, mylohyoid, and anterior belly of digastric. (Option D ruled out) Sensory component of Trigeminal Nuclei The motor component of Trigeminal Nuclei Carries pain, temperature, touch, pressure, and proprioception from the face. Main sensory nucleus - touch and pressure. (Option A ruled out) Spinal nucleus - pain and temperature. It extends till C2 of the spinal cord.

Mesencephalic nucleus - proprioception. The motor nucleus receives inputs from both cerebral hemispheres, the reticular formation, and the red nucleus and forms a reflex arc with the mesencephalic nucleus. Supplies muscles of mastication- Temporalis Masseter Lateral pterygoid Medial pterygoid Other muscles like Tensor tympani Tensor veli palatini Mylohyoid Anterior belly of digastric

questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding damage to the midline brainstem nuclei is false?

options.A: Damage to the oculomotor nucleus can result in the eye looking laterally and ptosis.
options.B: Injury to the trochlear nucleus leads to difficulty in upward gaze and may cause a compensatory head tilt to the same side.
options.C: Damage to the abducens nucleus results in medial strabismus, causing the affected eye to turn inward.
options.D: Lesion of the hypoglossal nucleus leads to weakness and atrophy of the tongue on the affected side.

explanation.text: Damage to the trochlear nucleus causes difficulty in downward and lateral gaze, often resulting in a compensatory head tilt to the opposite side. Lesions to Medial Brainstem Nuclei- Together form the somatic motor column (GSE) Oculomotor Nucleus (CN III): (Option A ruled out) The eye cannot move upward, downward, or inward. At rest, the eye is in a down-and-out position. The patient experiences double vision (diplopia).

The upper eyelid droops (ptosis) from paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris. The pupil is widely dilated and nonreactive to light due to paralysis of the sphincter pupillae and unopposed sympathetic dilator activity. Accommodation is impaired. Trochlear Nucleus (CN IV): Difficulty in downward and lateral gaze. Patients may exhibit a compensatory head tilt to the opposite side to manage diplopia (double vision).

Abducens Nucleus (CN VI): Medial strabismus (the affected eye cannot abduct), leading to horizontal diplopia. The affected eye is often turned inward. Diplopia is also seen. (Option C ruled out) Hypoglossal Nucleus (CN XII): Weakness of the tongue on the side of the lesion, causing atrophy and fasciculations. On protrusion, the tongue may deviate toward the affected side. (Option D ruled out)

questions.question: A 65 y/o patient presents with sudden dizziness, difficulty swallowing, ipsilateral loss of temperature sensation on the face, contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the trunk, ipsilateral ataxia, and giddiness. Which anatomical structure is responsible for the ipsilateral loss of temperature sensation on the face of this patient?

options.B: Spinal nucleus and tract of the trigeminal nerve
options.C: Inferior cerebellar peduncle

explanation.text: The patient is diagnosed with Wallenberg Syndrome due to the presence of ipsilateral loss of temperature sensation on the face, contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in the trunk, difficulty swallowing, ipsilateral ataxia, and giddiness. The spinal nucleus and tract of the trigeminal nerve are responsible for the ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the face, which is a hallmark feature of Wallenberg Syndrome.

Wallenberg Syndrome (Lateral Medullary Syndrome) Due to stroke or infarction in the lateral part of the medulla oblongata. Mainly due to occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA), a branch of the vertebral artery. Sometimes the vertebral artery directly supplies the lateral brainstem. Affects the dorsolateral aspect of the medulla and the inferior surface of the cerebellum.

Anatomical structure affected and features: Spinothalamic tract: Contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation of the trunk. (Option A ruled out) Spinal nucleus and tract of the trigeminal nerve: Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation of the face. Nucleus ambiguus: Ipsilateral paralysis of muscles of the palate, pharynx, and larynx.
Inferior cerebellar peduncle and cerebellum: Ipsilateral ataxia. (Option C ruled out) Vestibular nuclei: Giddiness. (Option D ruled out)

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect regarding Weber syndrome?

options.A: Lesion is in the oculomotor nerve fascicles and corticospinal fibers
options.B: Hemiplegia is present on the opposite side of the lesion
options.C: There is a lateral squint on the same side of the lesion

explanation.text: **Lesion is in the oculomotor nerve fascicles and corticospinal fibers (Option A):** Correct because Weber syndrome involves a midbrain lesion affecting the corticospinal tract and the oculomotor nerve fascicles.
**Hemiplegia is present on the opposite side of the lesion (Option B):** Correct because corticospinal fibers before decussation are damaged, causing contralateral hemiplegia.
**There is a lateral squint on the same side of the lesion (Option C):** Correct because oculomotor nerve palsy causes the eye to deviate laterally on the ipsilateral side.

**None of the above (Option D):** Correct answer since no statements are incorrect. Weber Syndrome: Topic Details Anatomy involved Midbrain ventral region (cerebral peduncle) affecting corticospinal tract and oculomotor nerve fascicles Lesion location Basis pedunculi of the midbrain Clinical features Ipsilateral oculomotor palsy (ptosis, pupil dilation, lateral deviation of eye) and contralateral hemiplegia Pathophysiology Damage to corticospinal tract causes contralateral hemiplegia; damage to oculomotor nerve fascicles causes ipsilateral third nerve palsy Signs Contralateral hemiplegia and ipsilateral third nerve pals

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect?

options.A: The PNS relays impulses in neurons away from the viscera.
options.B: The sympathetic nervous system has thoracolumbar outflow.
options.C: Erection is controlled by the parasympathetic nervous system.
options.D: Tearing is regulated by the parasympathetic nervous system.

explanation.text: In the parasympathetic system, the relay of impulses happens in neurons that are close to or directly within the target organs (viscera), not away from them.

Feature Parasympathetic Nervous System Sympathetic Nervous System Outflow Craniosacral outflow Thoracolumbar outflow (Option B ruled out) Preganglionic Neuron Located in the midbrain, pons, medulla oblongata, and S2–S4 segments of the spinal cord Located in the lateral horn of the spinal cord from Th 1–12 and L 1–2 segments Preganglionic Fibers Longer, myelinated Shorter, myelinated Relay of Impulses Occurs in neurons close to viscera Occurs in neurons a little away from the viscera they supply Postganglionic Fibers Short, nonmyelinated Long, nonmyelinated Neurotransmitter at Preganglionic Endings Acetylcholine Acetylcholine Neurotransmitter at Postganglionic Endings Acetylcholine Adrenaline (except sweat glands, where acetylcholine is used) Postganglionic Supply Only viscera are supplied, do not supply blood vessels of skeletal muscles All viscera are supplied; the exception is the suprarenal gland, which is supplied by preganglionic fibers Heart rate Decreased Increased Blood pressure Mildly decreased Increased Urinary bladder Voiding (decreased tone) Increased sphincter tone Bowel motility Increased Decreased motility Lungs Bronchoconstriction Bronchodilation Sweat glands - Sweating Pupils Constriction Dilation Sexual functions Erection (Option C ruled out) Ejaculation, orgasm Lacrimal glands Tearing (Option D ruled out) -

questions.question: Where does the hypothalamospinal tract terminate before synapsing with the second-order neurons?

options.C: Intermediolateral cell column of the spinal cord
options.D: Posterior horn of the spinal cord

explanation.text: The hypothalamospinal tract terminates in the intermediolateral cell column (IML) of the spinal cord, where it synapses with the second-order sympathetic neurons.

questions.question: All of the following options are branches of the internal carotid artery except?

options.C: Posterior communicating artery

explanation.text: Anterior inferior cerebellar artery is a branch of the basilar artery. The internal carotid artery is divided into three parts based on its course.

Petrous part Cavernous part Intracranial part Branches of the intracranial part of internal carotid artery: Branches Areas supplied Ophthalmic artery (Option A ruled out) Contents of orbit Posterior communicating artery (Option C ruled out) Crus cerebri, optic tract, hypophysis and hypothalamus Anterior choroidal artery (Option B ruled out) Crus cerebri and choroid plexus of inferior horn of

lateral ventricle Anterior cerebral artery Deep branches supply part of the internal capsule and the basal nuclei. Cortical branches supply the medial surface of the hemisphere. questions.question: A transverse section of the medulla oblongata at the level of the motor (pyramidal) decussation reveals modifications to the typical spinal cord structure. Which of the following changes is observed at this level?

options.A: Formation of the medial lemniscus from second-order axons
options.B: Crossing of corticospinal fibres from the anterior funiculi
options.C: Presence of the vestibular nuclei near the fourth ventricle
options.D: Appearance of the inferior olivary complex lateral to the pyramid

explanation.text: At the level of the motor decussation, corticospinal fibres cross from the anterior funiculi to the contralateral side, a hallmark of this level. Internal Organization of the Medulla Oblongata 1. Transverse Section at Motor (Pyramidal) Decussation Level The inferior medulla adapts to accommodate brainstem nuclei and fibres.

Corticospinal fibres cross at the motor decussation, decreasing the pyramid size. (Option B) Ventral grey column divides into: Supraspinal nucleus (first cervical nerve origin, continuous with the hypoglossal nerve nucleus). Nucleus of the accessory nerve (aligned with the nucleus ambiguus). Surrounding tracts: Ventral corticospinal tract (medioventral). Ventral and dorsal spinocerebellar tracts (dorsolateral).

Dorsal grey column modified by the presence of the nucleus gracilis and cuneatus, continuous with spinal structures. 2. Transverse Section at Sensory Decussation (Dorsal Column–Medial Lemniscus System) Nuclei and tracts present: Nucleus gracilis and nucleus cuneatus, receiving first-order afferent fibres.

Second-order axons (internal arcuate fibres) cross the midline as sensory decussation to form the medial lemniscus. (Option A ruled out) Medial lemniscus: Located dorsal to the pyramid. Inferior olivary complex appears lateral to it. (Option D ruled out) Other key structures: Dorsal spinocerebellar and trigeminal nerve tracts, reticular formation, corticospinal tract, medial longitudinal fasciculus, and tectospinal tract. 3.

Transverse Section at Caudal End of Fourth Ventricle Grey matter increases due to nuclei associated with cranial nerves IX, X, XI, and VIII. Key nuclei: Inferior olivary complex. Hypoglossal nucleus, vagus dorsal motor nucleus, salivatory nuclei, nucleus solitarius, and vestibular nuclei. (Option C ruled out) Restiform body forms the dorsal lateral border, carrying afferent fibers (spinocerebellar and olivocerebellar tracts).
Other structures: Spinal trigeminal nucleus, nucleus ambiguus, reticular formation. Spinocerebellar, spinothalamic, and rubrospinal tracts ventral to the olivary complex and pyramid.

questions.question: Which of the following findings is not a clinical manifestation of Wallenberg syndrome?

options.C: Ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss
options.D: Contralateral body pain and temperature loss

explanation.text: Ipsilateral ataxia is seen in Wallenburg sybdrome due to damage to inferior cerebellar peduncle, spino cerebellar tracts, and part of cerebellum. Wallenburg sybdrome: Also known as Lateral medullary syndrome Pathology: Blockage of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery. It supplies areas behind the inferior olivary nucleus. Damage to the lateral segment of the medulla posterior to the inferior olivary nucleus.

Clinical manifestation: Anatomical location Presenting clinical feature Nucleus ambiguous gives fibers to IX, X, and XI cranial nerves Ipsilateral paralysis of muscles of the soft palate, pharynx, and larynx Spinal nucleus and spinal tract of the trigeminal nerve Ipsilateral facial pain and temperature loss (Option C ruled out) Lateral spinothalamic tract Contralateral body pain and temperature loss (Option D ruled out) Vestibular nuclei Vertigo Inferior cerebellar peduncle, spino cerebellar tracts, and part of cerebellum Ipsilateral ataxia (Option A) Sympathetic fibres descend from the hypothalamus to cells in the lateral horn of spinal cord Horner’s syndrome (Option B ruled out), comprising ptosis, enophthalmos, miosis, and anhydrosis

questions.question: Which of the following nerve palsy would suggest a lesion affecting the structures within the interpeduncular fossa?

options.C: Oculomotor nerve

explanation.text: A lesion affecting the interpeduncular fossa could damage the oculomotor nerve (CN III), which emerges from this region, leading to diplopia and ptosis. Interpeduncular fossa It is a deep depression of the ventral surface of the midbrain between the two crura cerebri.

The lateral wall of the interpeduncular fossa bears the oculomotor sulcus, from which rootlets of the oculomotor nerve emerge from the brainstem and aggregate into a single fascicle. (Option C) Contents Oculomotor nerve (Option C) Circle of Willis Bifurcation of the basilar artery Peduncular segments of the posterior cerebral artery (PCA) and superior cerebellar artery, (SCA) Medial and lateral posterior choroidal arteries Basal vein of Rosenthal Glossopharyngeal nerve (Option A): and vagus nerve (Option B): The rootlets of the cranial nerves IX (Glossopharyngeal) and X (vagus) emerge through the posterolateral fissure, behind the olive.
**Hypoglossal nerve (Option D):** The rootlets of the hypoglossal nerve emerge from the anterolateral sulcus between the pyramid and the olive.
